early: Refrigerate pansy seeds — they need 7 days in the dark and cold before sowing.
Start cold-stratifying delphinium seeds in the fridge (7–14 days).
Cold-stratify lavender in damp perlite — it'll need 3–4 weeks.
Set up the heat mat and grow light. The season starts here.
mid: Surface sow all 30 rosemary seeds — they need light, and only half will make it.
Sow tomato sweetie on the heat mat at 24–27°C.
Sow calendula, aster, alyssum, and marigold — standard indoor conditions.
Sow snapdragon in the 16-tray — surface sow, no heat pad, keep it cool (15–18°C).
late: Check the pansy seeds — after 7 days in the fridge, sow them in a cool, dark spot (15°C).
Lavender should be surface sown under the grow light once stratified.
Raise the grow light to just above any seedlings that have emerged.
Monitor all trays for moisture — mist gently, don't drench.

early: Pre-soak parsley seeds 24 hours, then sow. They're slow — be patient.
Soak and scarify lupine seeds — careful, they're toxic to handle.
Sow basil (sweet, thai, tulsi) on the heat mat.
Sow oregano, thyme, chives, chamomile, yarrow, valerian, and mint — all surface sow.
mid: Cold-stratify echinacea 7 days, then sow in 16-tray in the dark.
Cold-stratify shiso 7–10 days, then sow.
Sow spinach and lettuce in the 16-tray — keep cool, no heat.
Sow swiss chard and kale — standard indoor conditions.
late: Sow arugula — it germinates fast.
Water from below to prevent damping off on all trays.
Begin diluted liquid fertilizer if you see true leaves appearing.
Check all march sowings for sprouts — thin any crowded seedlings.

early: Start hardening off seedlings: 1–2 hours outside in shade on Day 1, increase daily.
Protect from wind during hardening off — the seedlings aren't used to it yet.
Watch overnight temps — if below 5°C, use fleece or bring trays back in.
Buy lightweight potting mix and perlite (20–30% perlite to reduce container weight).
mid: May 15 — transplant day. Everything moves outside.
Confirm balcony layout: heaviest pots against the wall.
Plant tomato in the grow bag and set up the railing trellis immediately.
Water everything deeply after transplanting.
late: Train tomato horizontally from Day 1.
Direct sow cilantro and dill in C9B — keep dill far from tomato.
Soak nasturtium seeds 12–24 hours, then direct sow in C9.
Set up saucers under all containers.

early: Establish a daily watering routine — check soil moisture every morning.
Tomato gets liquid fertilizer weekly once flowers appear.
Pinch basil tips to encourage bushiness. Don't let it flower.
Deadhead pansies and marigolds to keep them blooming.
mid: First arugula and lettuce harvests should be ready.
Succession sow cilantro — it bolts fast in the warmth.
Check if any seedlings need potting up to larger containers.
Harvest basil, mint, and parsley regularly to encourage growth.
late: Keep deadheading weekly — calendula, pansies, marigolds.
Feed containers with diluted liquid fertilizer every two weeks.
Harvest shiso before it sets seed — it self-sows aggressively.
Watch the greens box closely in the heat.

early: Harvest tomatoes as they ripen — cherry tomatoes come in clusters.
Keep pinching basil — make pesto if there's too much.
Deadhead everything weekly to keep flowers coming.
Feed containers every 2 weeks.
mid: Harvest chamomile flowers when petals reflex downward — dry for tea.
Cut lavender when flowers just open — bundle and hang to dry.
Water in the evening during hot spells, not the morning.
Watch for heat stress — shade cloth if over 30°C.
late: Keep harvesting and deadheading — the garden is at peak production.
Succession sow cilantro again if it's bolted.
Dry oregano and thyme for winter stores.
Check the mint — it's probably trying to escape its pot.

early: Keep harvesting tomatoes — share extras with neighbours.
Dry herbs for winter: oregano, thyme, rosemary.
Harvest echinacea flowers at peak bloom for drying.
Collect calendula petals — they dry beautifully.
mid: Make tulsi tea from fresh leaves — this is peak flavour.
Sow a late round of arugula and lettuce for the fall harvest.
Continue deadheading and feeding containers.
Check for powdery mildew in humid weather.
late: Take a midsummer garden photo — you'll want to remember this.
Keep watering deeply in the evenings.
Harvest any remaining chamomile for drying.
Watch the kale — it's about to come into its own.

early: Harvest remaining tomatoes — green ones ripen on the windowsill.
Enjoy the asters and snapdragons — they love cool weather.
Start saving seeds from calendula, nasturtium, and marigold.
Final herb harvest for drying and freezing.
mid: Reduce watering as temperatures drop.
Harvest valerian roots if this is year 2+.
The kale is sweeter after a light frost — keep harvesting.
Bring rosemary and lavender inside before the first frost warning.
late: Start thinking about wrapping up the season.
Keep harvesting kale, chard, and spinach — they're cold-hardy.
Clean and dry any empty pots.
Make notes about what worked and what to change next year.

early: Harvest the last of everything.
Empty and clean all containers.
Compost spent soil or store it for refreshing next spring.
Bring any remaining perennials inside for winter.
mid: Clean and store pots, trays, and tools.
Make sure rosemary is in a bright window — it needs light over winter.
Export garden data as a backup.
Write down what you learned this season.
late: Rest. You grew a garden on a balcony.
Start dreaming about next year.
Order seed catalogues if you're feeling ambitious.
The lavender and rosemary are your only charges now — water sparingly.

march: Damping off is the biggest risk right now — don't overwater seedlings, and make sure air circulates.
Rosemary has a very low germination rate (30–50%). Don't panic if nothing appears for weeks.
Snapdragon and pansy need cool conditions — keep them away from the heat mat.
Check that cold-stratifying seeds in the fridge stay damp but not soaking.
april: Damping off risk continues — water from below, not above.
Watch for leggy seedlings — raise the grow light if stems are stretching.
Lupine seeds are toxic — wash hands after handling.
Parsley is famously slow to germinate. Don't give up on it.
may: Last frost is May 15 — don't move anything outside before hardening off.
Watch overnight temps during hardening off. Below 5°C means fleece or bring trays in.
Wind is the hidden danger for new transplants — shelter them for the first week.
Dill and tomato are enemies — keep them in separate containers.
june: Aphids appear early in the season — check nasturtiums and roses daily.
Cilantro bolts fast in the heat. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks to always have fresh.
Basil flowers mean the plant is stressed or mature — pinch them immediately.
Watch lettuce and spinach for bolting as temperatures climb.
july: Heat stress is real above 30°C — shade cloth protects delicate greens.
Powdery mildew can appear in humid weather — check leaf undersides.
Keep an eye on the mint — it will try to escape its isolation pot.
Tomato blossom end rot means inconsistent watering — keep it steady.
august: Powdery mildew thrives in humid, warm weather — improve air circulation.
Spider mites appear in hot, dry conditions — mist foliage in the morning.
Harvest shiso before it drops seeds — it self-sows everywhere.
Watch for caterpillars on the kale and chard.
september: First frost can sneak up — watch the forecast and have fleece ready.
Bring rosemary and lavender inside at the first hint of frost.
Rotting fruit left on plants attracts pests — pick everything, even if small.
Valerian attracts cats — the roots especially. Keep the pot somewhere safe during harvest.
october: Rosemary needs a bright window indoors — south-facing is ideal.
Don't overwater indoor plants through winter — they need much less.
Clean pots thoroughly to prevent overwintering pests and disease.
Store saved seeds in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.
